utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. McCormack, the Chamber is happy to see you here. In view of the assignment, we think that you should be here as often as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCORMACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I'm sure it will be helpful to the Chamber when we come to the final stages of this trial. Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have a couple of matters to return to in 1998, but let's move otherwise immediately to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry we're a little delayed this morning, but it won't inconvenience you beyond this initial, I think -- it won't delay you further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us when giving evidence in chief, and I can't quote the precise words to you, that killing people in the course of dealing with terrorists was the absolute last resort, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be around it. The point was always to bring terrorists into custody or to have the problem resolved in a different way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Lieutenant Colonel Blagoje Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was head of the police department in the Secretariat of the Interior of Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, please, at this exhibit, 319, tab 32. You have the original. You'll see this is a document which comes from Djordjevic, approved by your police chief boss, Borislav Vlahovic. If we look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort, could you just show the last page of this document in English on the overhead projector, please. Nothing coming up on the overhead projector so far as I'm concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we see that it was compiled by Djordjevic, and then underneath that, Mr. Nort, approved by Vlahovic. So if we now go back, please, to the first page, we see something right at the top that relates to your territory. "Pursuant to the agreement with members of the Secretariat of the Interior in Djakovica and members of the Department of State Security of the SUP of the Interior in Pec and Djakovica ..." And then it says, "Ambush plan," under "Objective," "To prevent --" I'm sorry. We see under "Time of Execution" that it's forecasting ambushes to be set up from the 24th to the 31st of January, 1999, and this ambush plan then says as the objective: "To prevent the movement of terrorists on the above-mentioned local road, eliminate the said terrorists ..." Nothing about capturing them. What do you say to that? By 1999 it wasn't a question of capturing terrorists, it was a question of liquidating them, wasn't it, if you could?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that this paper that is before me was not signed by Blagoje Djordjevic, as you pointed out. Next, it wasn't signed by Colonel Borislav Vlahovic, and I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question on the basis of this exhibit, and I'll ask you to look now at the next paragraph as well, "General Tasks." "Monitor the said road, as well as other local roads running from the direction of Jablanica and Bucane villages in order to spot in timely fashion the above-mentioned vehicles and any other vehicles used by terrorists, and upon identification of the vehicles and their passengers, use concentrated fire to neutralise and eliminate them."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot speak about this. As I said, this is a plan that I'm totally unfamiliar with. I'm totally unfamiliar with it being drafted by Blagoje Djordjevic, as you said, or signed by Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or Vlahovic, rather, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I am not aware of any of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on this document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on this document, Mr. Nort, page 3 in English, Roman V, "Preparations for Execution," for you, please, Mr. Paponjak. It's right, isn't it, that one of the significant characteristics of those you described as the terrorists was that they used Chinese ammunition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about right now. Terrorists for the most part did use Chinese ammunition. That's what facts indicate. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see under here "Preparations for Execution," and this is for execution in the elimination of KLA: "On the 23rd of January, 1999, the platoon leader and squad leaders of the PJP, together with sector leader from Celopek shall make a reconnaissance of the area and the ambush locations. The platoon leader of PJP shall provide grenade launchers and ammunition manufactured in China ..." Why should your local organisation be demanding that elimination exercises should be done with weaponry of Chinese manufacture? Would that be in order to be able to cast blame for what happened on the KLA if things went wrong?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not the kind of assignment that was given at all. This material was probably drafted with that objective in mind. This is not a plan of the SUP in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you could remind me how we dealt with the authenticity of this document. I think this is part of Mr. Coo's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was found by the OTP in the police station at Pec in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm trying to understand the question you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there evidence that the KLA used weaponry of Chinese manufacture?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A lot of evidence that the weaponry and ammunition typically associated with the KLA was of Chinese manufacture. I can't point Your Honour, I'm afraid, immediately to an instance, but I think there's plenty of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, we haven't yet dealt with the heart of the allegation against those in Pec in authority at the time, namely that you and your colleagues engaged in straightforward and well-organised ethnic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I get a copy of this document that Mr. Nice has just shown to the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let a copy be passed to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused will realise, of course, that it is an existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your colleagues, Mr. Paponjak, engaged in straightforward and very well organised ethnic cleansing before the bombing -- organised before the bombing even started. You realise that's the allegation against you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there are accusations of this kind, but that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it? And you did it under the supervision or instruction of your superiors, tracking back to Belgrade and to this accused, let me make it quite clear. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear what you're trying to say, but quite simply that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to summarise for you in just a few sentences some of the evidence we've heard with some dates, for your comment. On the 23rd of March, according to a witness Zatriqi, MUP officers from Pec took three of his buses which they later used to transport people from the city. On the 25th of March, according to the witness Sokoli, he saw police from Pec burning and looting houses. He was beaten by Serb forces. He was loaded on a truck and sent to Prizren --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should these be questions rather than speeches by the Prosecutor as to the nature of his case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can turn them all into questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're putting these matters to the witness -- perhaps you should put them individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can, but with your leave there's no need to do so. I've indicated that I'm just putting our case comprehensively and in the shortest possible time so that the witness can know the nature of the evidence. I suspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Put them collectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that Mr. Sokoli said he was beaten, loaded onto a truck and forced out; and finally, on the 27th of March, according to a witness Mr. Konaj, he was also kicked out, told by policemen that there was no place for him to go other than to Montenegro. Now, that's, in very short order, a summary of some of the evidence, and I want to know from you, Mr. Paponjak, whether you allow for the possibility of police officers in your town doing that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes it's possible that you have rogue elements in a police force doing bad things. Do you think even a rogue policeman could have tried to force Kosovo Albanians out of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "wild elements" in the police? I worked with these people for years. I know them. Had anybody been wild, they would have been eliminated from the police in the way in which this was prescribed, by taking disciplinary action, et cetera. There was no one who went wild in the police. Since this gentleman said that the policemen took away three buses from him, he probably knows which policeman did that, and he probably gave their names, and then we'll know exactly whether these were policemen to begin with and how these buses were taken away from him and what happened to the buses. He certainly knew all the policemen in Pec because there weren't very many of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep saying some policemen or some forces, but they know all of our names; our names, surnames, our other characteristics. They know who these policemen were, if they were policemen, and then it will be easy to track them down by name and surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Come to that further, probably in a second, but no movement, then, of Kosovo Albanians by the police. Was there at the middle, end of March, beginning of April, was there any organised movement of any part of the population by any force, police or military?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, you see, you've described the movement of people right at the end of March and the confusion in the centre of Pec with you moving the traffic on as sort of well-meaning but unfortunate chaos. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There was quite a bit of disorder, rather, commotion in the roads. That's true. There were even bottlenecks on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd be good enough, then, to have a look at Exhibit 319, tab 36, with me. And if I may say so, this is not a document that should have come to you as a surprise, for it's been published in easily available public material since 2001. Now, this is an order, Mr. Paponjak, and if you'd like, please, Mr. Nort, to take us to the last page, we'll see that it's signed by Colonel Dusko Antic, so we can see whose it is. There he is. And now let's go back to the first page, please. It's dated the 30th of March, 1999, Mr. Paponjak. What it says is this: "On the basis of the Supreme Commander's order on the declaration of a state of war and the moving of a part of the population out of the zone of responsibility of the Pec VO ..." Would you tell us what "moving of a part of the population out of the zone of responsibility" means, since you've told us that there was no organised movement of any part of the population by any force.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who is involved in military or police work knows what this means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you tell us.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a state of war, combat activities are anticipated. That is to say that the population has to be moved out of the area of responsibility in order to protect their lives in case there is combat action. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at defence positions there cannot be any civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, didn't I give you an adequate opportunity in the last question but three to tell us whether there was any movement of any part of the population? Didn't I give you an adequate chance to give us an account of this then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked that in terms of the setting up of columns and whatever else there was, not in terms of the measures that have to be taken by the army and the police. This is an absolutely normal thing that is done in any situation where there is a state of war. Where combat action is anticipated, the population is moved out of the war zone. It is relocated. It's not moved out altogether, but it is relocated to safe areas, and that is done anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you in the clearest terms was there any -- was there at the middle, end of March, beginning of April, was there any organised movement of any part of the population by any force, military or police, and you said no. Mr. Paponjak, this document shows you to be a liar, and you've lied throughout your evidence to this Court, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your wish to have that said and to say that. That's quite clear, and that's clear to everyone who is listening. I never lied, sir, not a single point in time. I understand that you have that kind of wish to say that, but no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many thousand Kosovo Albanians, on your estimate, voluntarily left their homes between, say, the end of March and June of 1999, how many thousand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not involved in such estimates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the population of Pec before the conflict? You're a policeman, you might know that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might know had they taken part in the census. However, the Albanians did not take part in the census so we don't have this information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No idea at all of the number of police you were policing? Was it a hundred, or a thousand, or 5.000? You give us a clue.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean estimates of the total population, what our estimates were, what my personal estimates were, I can give you that. However, I cannot give you any accurate figures. No one can. Estimates vary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, just before we depart from that document, if we are, are you saying that no part of the population was moved out of the zone of responsibility of the Pec VO, or are you saying that there was a point at which a part of the population was moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot claim either. I assume that all the inhabitants, Serbs and Albanians, were relocated from all the positions that were taken by the army of Yugoslavia or members of the MUP of Serbia at places where positions were supposed to be organised in terms of personnel, equipment, where the defence positions were supposed to be. The population was relocated from these areas with a view to protecting their own lives. In case there are combat activities, civilian casualties wanted to be prevented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand that answer. Were you not in such a position of responsibility that you would know one way or another whether this order ever came to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such measures were taken by commanders and leaders of units. That is why I was not in a position to know that. Every leader of a unit or commander of a unit organising his positions does that. That is why I assumed that this had been done indeed. When deploying his personnel, when fortifying the positions, digging the trenches, et cetera, the commander of the unit or the leader of the unit takes such measures. If there are civilians nearby, he has to relocate them to a different position, a safe position, and that is ultimately decided. My work was completely different. I don't even know where the positions were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to take up too much time, but I really don't understand that answer at all, because the wording of this order is the moving of a part of the population out of the zone of responsibility of the Pec VO. That's not just a movement a short distance away, that's a movement out of your zone of responsibility. Would you not know if that had happened? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not say moving out now in this document. It says relocation of the population. I don't know how it was translated in the document that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need to argue about these words, but do you not have in Serbian the words "out of the zone of responsibility of the Pec VO"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It says "and relocation of a part of the population from the zone of responsibility," not "out of the zone of responsibility," and I would like it translated verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it's not the same. That refers to the population of that area. Relocation of the population of that area, not from outside. So relocation within the same zone. Moving out would mean moving people out of that area. Relocation, for instance, within this room would mean re-seating of a person, whereas moving out would mean that the person is leaving the room altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But relocation of someone from this room would mean moving a person out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will remain a mystery for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: VO is a military organisation, Vojni Okrug, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, you heard me summarise the evidence of a few witnesses, and there have been other witnesses who have said they were forced out of Pec. In light of your answers to His Honour and to me, would this be reasonable: There is no scope for them being even remotely accurate or honest in their account. Either they are completely wrong or you're completely wrong. Would you accept that? You were there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's no scope for them making an honest mistake of thinking they'd been forced out, thinking they'd seen houses being burned down by the police, of thinking that they had been threatened that had to leave or they'd be killed. There's no scope for genuine mistake, is there? Either they are wrong or you're wrong.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I am right, and I don't know what they were thinking and why they were doing what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The trouble for you is there are two problems for you and one of them is this: Your answers to me and your recent answers to His Honour Judge Bonomy simply don't get round the fact that when you were asked in specific terms, "Was there any organised movement of any part of the population by any force?" you said no, and on your latest answers that itself would be untrue and, therefore, a lie.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Here again, the reference is not to moving by force. It is a reference to a relocation or moving for the purpose of protection of those people. They're moving from a place where their lives could be in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us this, because you've been able to help the accused and the Court with a certain amount of conjecture from time to time about people being shot while trying to escape from Dubrava and things like that. The Court's heard a lot of evidence about people being compelled to give up their identification documents at borders when they left for Albania, sometimes for Macedonia. What conceivable reason was there for police, maybe from your own authority, taking, perhaps as gifts, the identification documents of these departing Kosovo Albanians? What reason could there be for that happening, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have now give us -- given us an account which is very difficult to follow. First of all, you said I helped the accused by saying that people were escaping from being shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you know -- let's just deal with this. No, Mr. Paponjak, just wait. You've known about this indictment for years; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To every direct question you will receive a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've known about this indictment for years.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, in your questions --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've known about this indictment for years. You referred to it in one of your signed documents as an exhibit. You've known about this document for years; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not in dispute. The indictment has been in existence for years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have known for years, as has everybody else interested in this conflict, that it is alleged the Serbs kicked the Kosovo Albanians out of their country. You've known that for years.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Known about the allegation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have known, because of course you looked at the indictment, or someone in your team did, and you will have heard the evidence in preparation for this case, that one of the major allegations, because it's an important bit of evidence, is that Kosovo Albanians were compelled by police and military to hand over their documents of identification, their car number plates, and so on. You've known that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that have to do with my testimony?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer the question, because you're giving evidence. You have known that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't know about these allocations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is this: When I ask you a very simple question to give your explanation for something that you've known about for years and you must have turned your mind to, why do you choose to take time with a long discursive answer? I want you to tell these Judges what conceivable reason there could be for Kosovo Albanians to hand in or to have taken from them their documents of identification. Will you now please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know the documents were taken from them. I have nothing to do with Prizren, which seems to be your claim, and you are trying to put to me now that I knew about it, and you want me to comment on something I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This much is true and obvious, isn't it: Despite knowing all these allegations for years, your documents, which I must suggest are a sham, your documents show no investigation into these allegations of any kind, do they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not in the jurisdiction of the Pec SUP, and we cannot investigate into things that allegedly happen in some other area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't think, by any chance, there's a touch of bureaucracy in your answers, do you? Don't you have an imagination or an idea of things that happened outside the area of your SUP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has answered the question, Mr. Nice. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, then, please, this: Why did Zoran Aleksic leave the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly know who he was, don't you? Don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which Zoran Aleksic. But if you mean -- let me think. Zoran Aleksic was one of our employees. We had a person by that name, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did. After all, if all the -- if all the inhabitants of Pec should know all the policemen, then certainly all the policemen should know all the policemen, and Zoran Aleksic is one of them. We can just see him, just so we can be quite sure that he exists, on, for example, tab 20.2, only one of a number of examples. Shall we look at that, tab 20.2. Just put it on the overhead projector. Actually, here it is. Have my copy. Just see it. Just see that his signature's there. Signs off on one of the documents. I can't tell you what it is because it's not translated. Doesn't matter. What is he, a captain, or was he a captain?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know almost --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that having what -- did he move with you from Kosovo to Kragujevac or was he deployed elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall at this moment what happened to him, where he was transferred, but he was from the section of crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you become aware that he'd left the territory? Again, the -- this is such a small territory that you'd expect people to know the policemen, you must be able to give us some clue as to what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid my answer will have to be a little longer again. The Secretariat of the Interior of Pec had 800 employees, organised into sections. Within a section you have chiefs and heads of departments, and they are in charge of the employees under them. There are several departments - at least three - so you have chiefs of departments and his deputies. I, as head of the secretariat, rarely had the opportunity to deal with individuals except in very exceptional cases. Normally I had no knowledge about any particular individual. At the time, the situation in Pec was very chaotic. It took us several months to relocate and find a new location and find accommodation for our employees, whether with family or otherwise. And as people found a way to move to the new location, they reported back to me and continued to work in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which is my immediate concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's coming to that. You're coming to that now, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I cannot give you any information about hundreds of other employees either, because I was not in charge of any individual in particular. My job was to organise conditions of work in a new place, and chiefs of sections or departments reported to me about their employees and their lines of work. Perfectly by chance I know that Zoran Aleksic relocated to Cacak because he lived in Cacak, but I learned about that through private channels more than official ones because I myself coming from Cacak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you learnt about him and about his onward movement from Cacak.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he lived in Cacak, that his father lived there as well, because I visited his father at home several times, and I know that at some point he left the service and moved out of Cacak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he leave the service, Mr. Paponjak, because he was concerned to tell the truth about and to blow the whistle on the Pec policemen and he was hounded out by threats?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And who was allegedly threatening him?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other Serbian policemen.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Aleksic had a perfectly normal, good relationship with me and he never told me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to another topic. At the beginning of June of 1999, you were still in service in Pec, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was an operation in Pec at the beginning of June of 1999 to dig up the bodies of people who had been killed by Serbs between March and June, involving the police, you would have known about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Now, please tell the Judges when it happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it happened. You are now trying to put it to me that it did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me suggest to you that the following at least were involved in this operation: Your head, Boro Vlahovic; a man called Bato Bulatovic; Milojevic Mladen and Zoran Stanisic, those last two being respectively head of the criminal division and chief of the technical division of your police. They and many others, no doubt, were involved in digging up the bodies and sending them off to Batajnica in Serbia. You knew about it and you were involved, and I'd like you now please to tell the Judges a bit more about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. While you're at it you can say that I dug them up personally. Nothing like that happened, and I didn't participate in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, may we take it, then, that if in due course there is evidence to show that bodies were dug up at the time that I've suggested, with the assistance in particular of the traffic police, that's something that you would have known of?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything of the sort because it did not happen. I didn't know anything about it, and even less could I say that I participated myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Kosovo Albanians do you say were killed by Serb forces in the course of the bombing campaign between March and June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said more than once already that Serb forces did not kill Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not one solitary Kosovo Albanian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to take very much of your time or the Court's on that, but just again look at one picture, please, in the book "Under Orders," which as I said yesterday makes the point that all the crimes alleged against -- not all, many of the crimes alleged against those ethnically cleansing in Pec were well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just the photograph, please, and the caption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here's something. Look at the photograph, please, and I'll read the caption slowly so you can follow it: "Witnesses identified the man on the right as Nebojsa Minic, known as 'Mrtvi' ('Death'). He is implicated in the extortion and killing of six family members in Pec on June the 12th. On the left is Vidomir Salipur, a Pec policeman and alleged head of the Munja gang, who was killed by the KLA on April 8, 1999. The date and location of the photograph are unknown." Did you as a policeman remain totally ignorant of the person known as Nebojsa Minic who is dealt with in great detail -- or some detail in the pages of this book? Did you remain ignorant of him throughout?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Vidomir Salipur, who is on the photo here. I don't know the other person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right that Vidomir Salipur was head of something called the Munja gang, which was a paramilitary group that went around and killed people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said loud and clear that it was a policeman, Vidomir Salipur. I don't know what gang you are referring to in connection with this policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No investigations into the sort of allegations that we see in this publicly available material by your police force in exile, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no reports or other information about this. I don't know where this material is coming from and how this photo was made in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've had evidence from the United Nations Commissioner for Refugees, through a witness, that on the 12th of April, a total of some 3.600 refugees from Istok and other municipalities arrived at Montenegro. From your sighting of the chaos in the centre of town when you were directing the traffic, or whatever you were doing, does it seem sensible to you that some 3.000 people from the neighbouring municipalities of Istok might have found their way to Montenegro on the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean do I find it reasonable?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to have a picture of what you were doing, Mr. Paponjak, and as far as I can understand it - forgive me if I have got it wrong - you were doing your best in town to control the traffic and to help people move along the roads. You must, as an experienced traffic policemen, have had some idea of the numbers of people you were dealing with. Do you think for all these communities under your general control some 12.000 might have found their way to Albania by -- sorry, to Montenegro by about the 12th of April? That's all. Does that seem reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they have been able to find their way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another 2.000 going to Montenegro. Does that seem about right, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction towards Montenegro was overcrowded all the time because it's an uphill road. You have to go through the Kula pass, movement is very slow. People travelled in ox carts, cars tractors and on foot. That thoroughfare was very busy. There were bottlenecks, but the column was moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I've given you a chance to answer the question and I'm going to move back, as I said, to one event in 1998. We looked at it in tab 1.4 yesterday, and this is the Salihaj incident. You took us to 1.4, number -- I thought it was number 56. Perhaps you will remind me of which number it is for the Salihajs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 59.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be good enough, now that we've got 59 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've got 59 on the overhead projector, perhaps read it out for us. It's not very long. That's the only way we can see what you say there. Read it out for us, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an incident that happened in Susica, Istok municipality, on the 9th of August, 1998. "On the 9th of August, 1998, around 600 hours, a terrorist attack was carried out against the police patrol of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in the village of Susica, Istok municipality. Members the police responded to the fire and on that occasion killed eight members of the KLA, namely, Saban Salihaj, Hisen Salihaj, Abedin, Miljazim, Isa, Hisniju; Arben and Gashi Nazmi, who carried out terrorist attacks against citizens and members of the MUP in that area from May to August, 1998. On-site investigation was performed by investigating judge of the district court in Pec, Veselin Trajinovic. External examination of the corpses was performed by Dr. Milivoje Stijovic. The corpse was turned over to the family for funeral upon orders of the investigating judge. Report KU number 270/98, 291, 291 and DR/98 were submitted to the district public prosecutor of Pec."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's it, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry: "Attachment case file with records number A/III-59."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have that case file here with us today?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here, not today. Behind short reports like this are case files in our archive. There are about 1.000 such case files.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, your very bare report that you rely on here in this document doesn't tell us, does it, which of these alleged terrorists was 75 years old. Can you tell us which one it was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of them, but in the case file there are the records of the on-site investigation and various other notes that are attached there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that one of them was 16 years old. You can't deny that, can you? You haven't got any material to back up your brief summary.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material isn't here, but the material does exist and you can receive it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I can also suggest to you, because it's reported and documented elsewhere, that one of the women was abducted and her body, she having been killed, was only found later, days later. This wasn't an attack on terrorists. If it involved one member of the KLA, it was a revenge attack carried out by police from your police station. Who led the attack on these so-called terrorists? Was it you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, not a single woman was abducted or killed. Secondly, it wasn't an attack --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the official documents, from the records compiled by the investigating judge relating to her on-site investigation and other official notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this one of the files you've reviewed in detail or did you leave this one to the team, or do you know about it personally, Mr. Paponjak? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looked at a videotape from the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that show? Did it show the 16-year-old or the 75-year-old? Did it show the slit throats?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall anything that's inconvenient, do you? That's my suggestion to you as to your evidence in general. You've always got an alibi for anything that's inconvenient. Isn't that the reality of how you've been giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just said is not true. The unfortunate images we saw here, some of which I saw when I was on the spot. So the footage we saw here is also unfortunate or, if you like, inconvenient, but I don't deny them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn, then, to imagery, and let's go to Dubrava. Just remind ourselves that the documents on Dubrava are tab -- tab 8, and the supporting material is on -- much later on; tab 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: File 7, if the Chamber is interested in reminding itself what is contained there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Dicklich to play, in order to save time, the Dubrava tape that the accused has produced in parts, and I'll make some propositions as the tape is being played and then ask the witness questions at the end of each section.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, you appreciate, don't you, that there is no dispute but that NATO bombed the prison on the 19th of May. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's not something that is challenged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that there has been regular assertions by NATO, indeed by witnesses - I'm not going to take you through it all - that Dubrava prison was used as military or police or special police base in the period leading up to the conflict and indeed during the conflict? You understand that's always been asserted?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly that is what is said, but that was not the case, and probably it was the terrorists that planted that information on NATO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You appreciate that you've already told us you've never been to Dubrava prison yourself before your visit on the 19th, and therefore you have no personal knowledge of what the prison complex was used for; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, I didn't inspect the prison, but quite certainly we didn't have any of our forces there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So any witness who says that there were forces operating from there or from near there has got it completely wrong; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first tape which we'll now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're using Sanction, by the way, Your Honours, for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first tape that we -- sorry, the first part of the tape relates to the 19th of May. On Sanction. We'll make sure it's working for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have it being displayed?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what we see is that this is an apparently proper document with -- showing the bodies carefully numbered. The video is timed 16:37, 16:38, and dated. In your experience as a police officer, this would appear to be a proper forensic video of a scene of crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we move on, we see there's quite a concentration - and I'll ask Ms. Dicklich to move on and find it - of the damage that was done, in particular the prisoners breaking down the doors. We'll find that a little bit later. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point is an obvious one and is made in publications which reveal the prisoners spending an hour and a half to break down the doors. Why did nobody let them out? Do you know? Why did the guards not unlock the door and let them out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't know. Maybe the guards had moved away and gone into safety to protect themselves from the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They couldn't be bothered to go -- did you not inquire? Did nobody inquire as to the guards, How come you didn't let the prisoners out? How come you let them die where they were bombed? Did nobody ask that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should I be the one to ask that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you wouldn't be the one to ask it, tell us who should have asked it and then we'll see if it turns up in anybody else's report. You went there. You're a senior policeman. You've come here to give evidence about Dubrava. Forgive my asking you how it comes that nobody bothered to ask why they weren't unlocked before their hour and a half scramble to get out.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of our arrival, they weren't on the premises any more. Why would I then ask why nobody had let them out if they weren't in there in the first place when I arrived?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, in your tab 8 you record the fact that as soon as the attack was over the police and medical team came to the site. Yes, no inquiry as to that. Let's move on to the 21st of May. That's the second video. And to remind everybody, there were two phases of bombing on the 21st of May; morning and then later on. This one, again we see it's a properly prepared video. It's got a date. It's at a slow-ish, measured speed. It's got a time on it, 11:57 we can see at the moment. And is it right - you've seen this slowly and asked us to look at it slowly - it deals with the damage to the infrastructure, a hole in the wall near the heating plant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does show, I think, the prisoners. It shows the prisoners against the wall. And we've had evidence that after the bombing, after the first bombing on the 19th, we've had evidence that the prisoners were kept in the yard overnight, it being obviously safer so far as potential bombing is concerned, to be in the open and not in a building that might be targeted. You know nothing to counter the evidence that the prisoners were taken out after the bombing on the 19th and allowed to sleep in the yard thereafter, do you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any of those facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that there were found in the open air mattresses and bodies is consistent with the mattresses having come out after the 19th and not being brought out for any other purpose than for people to sleep on after the first bombing, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That just means that they were there. Now, whether they were let out or they got out themselves is a matter of speculation, and I'm sure that those providing security for the prison would know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me a minute and we shall be able to get there, but it's quite difficult to select small passages from a long video. There we are. Now, I think -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a part of this video, the video on the 21st, the time is -- I can't quite see, but it doesn't matter. And over by the wall, though, we see lots of people moving around in comparative freedom. Do you understand that would be the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move to the -- and we know that this, then, ended. People -- there were journalists there, I think, and everybody ran away, apart from the prisoners, maybe, when the bombing began again. And we then come to the third video, which is -- let's have a look at it. The first thing to notice about this video, Mr. Paponjak, and I'd like your comment on this straight away, is it hasn't got a date on it. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably at the time the date recorder wasn't switched on or a different camera was used, because it was filmed over several days. So perhaps a different camera was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pausing there for a minute. You made the point that it was important for your people to be at scenes like this immediately after things had happened, and as you were on the 19th and as you were on the -- not you, I mean collective you, were on the 21st. You're now trying to suggest, although you have no evidence of it, that there was further bombing on the 22nd and 23rd. If there was such bombing on the 22nd and 23rd, can you explain why the MUP didn't go and look at it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't make anybody go, force them after what they had experienced on the 21st. Who could you find? And who would be the person to make them, force them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer. I want to check with you whether it's imagination or reality. Have you got any statement from anybody saying that? Have you got a police report saying, "I, Captain So-and-so, tried to get people to go to the prison and they wouldn't go"? Have you? Or are you making it up as you go along, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not making it up. You asked my opinion, and I'm giving you it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask your opinion. I asked you to explain something. You're the man who has come with all the documents and all the reports. You claim from time to time to have looked at parts of the supporting material. If there's any ambiguity in my questioning, let me clarify it. I want you, please, now to point to a single piece of material that suggests efforts to go and inspect the bombing on the 22nd and 23rd were thwarted by fear. Do you follow the question? Let's have the answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said to you now I would not be the person to send anybody there, after what the on-site investigation team experienced on the 21st, for as long as there were planes flying overhead and for as long as there was bombing, because that would have meant that I was sending people to a certain death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's understand this. When you went -- when whoever went to take this video on the 24th, had you established a direct line of communication with NATO so that they told you there was going to be no more bombing? Had Jamie Shea rung you up to say that's it for bombing of Dubrava prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assume that at that time there were no flights and so the people monitoring the situation had ascertained that there were no flights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you know about that? You didn't know about the early ones until they happened. How could you know? You're making it up as you go along, Mr. Paponjak, aren't you, because you'll do anything to try and help this accused.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that we didn't have any reconnaissance teams and teams to monitor the situation and report back about flights and the general situation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that evidenced in the Dubrava file? Can I find it so that we can check it out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the Dubrava file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we press on with this video. One of the things about it is that the video shows - and I'm not asking you to do it now because it would take too long - very little change in the damage to buildings when compared with the earlier 21st. For example, we have a couple of stills, if you want to have a look at them we can put them on the overhead projector, for the 21st and the 24th. Perhaps we could just do that now. Stop the thing for the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is to make a point, I don't need them to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at these two of the heating plant, I think it is. One shows the 21st. It's a still from the videos. You have to trust us on that. Can we see that on the -- we're still on Sanction, I'm afraid. So you can just switch to the overhead projector. There's one on the 21st. Let's have a look at the one on the 24th, if it is the 24th. The other one, please, Mr. Nort. Very little difference in the damage to the principal buildings of interest, was there? Was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want my comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a civil engineer should perhaps take a look at this and give you an answer, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just of interest, the Prosecution's own case, the witness Jacky Rowland said there was a significant change in the buildings from her visit from the 21st and when she arrived on the 24th, which is in her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, there was one -- there was one building indeed which was damaged. We can come to that if you want to have a look at it, and I know that His Honour Judge Kwon's interested in looking at the canteen. Yes. But also the damage that Jacky Rowland saw is consistent with damage by grenades that may have been thrown. Can we go back to Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we look at this video without the date, and we're playing it in its realtime, I think, at the moment. This doesn't have anything about it, does it, of the sort of professional nature of the first two videos. It starts off fairly slowly but gets rapidly much faster in its survey of bodies. Do you remember that, Mr. Paponjak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at the time. I assume that they were trying to film it all as soon as possible to be able to leave the area and that they were planning to do a more lengthy job later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... area? I thought you'd told us that they would no doubt have found it safe to be there knowing there were no flights. Why would they want to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived it was safe, but there was always the danger of planes flying overhead again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just turn now to a few particular details. What does this show? What does this show?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recognise what it shows but I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the canteen with the hole in the ceiling but no bodies underneath? Was it? And here's the canteen again. Actually, you can see it again. There you are, the canteen damage but no sign of any bodies being killed as a result of that bomb. You can see the tables and the chairs. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's look at the -- well, you've brought this video and apparently you can say something about it and I'm going to ask you at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. end what you can say about it, but let's have a look at some of the bodies with dates on them. We again have stills. I think we can just satisfy you as to -- here's a body, and here is the still from the body. I can lay it on the overhead projector. It's clear, isn't it, that the naming and date of death of bodies was recorded by other people at the prison, prisoners and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can't see it. The ELMO is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see here that this one, Eminazeri -- it's not very clear as we can see it but we can hand a copy in. The date here is given for death at Dubrava of the 23rd of May. Did you notice that as you reviewed this film?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is improper because Mr. Nice claims that that is the date of death, whereas it can be the date at which the body was brought up from the rubble. It can be any other date. It doesn't say that it was the date of death. It just says the 23rd of May. Perhaps it was the date when the body was filmed, for example. And he starts out from the assumption that it was the actual date of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we just look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did the witness say in answer to that? Did you have a comment on Mr. Nice's question about the date, that it was the date of death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to say that I don't know what it means or who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Milosevic, the point you have made can also be made in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, we've got copies of this for the Chamber and it may be to save -- we haven't. Sorry. But I'll hand one in. You can see on the screen that the last word is "Dubrava." So we've got, Mr. Paponjak, a date, and you've got the accused's intervention to help you with your imagination, we've then got a name, and then we've got some figures. And what language is that all written in, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this will be something from my imagination again but I said clearly yesterday that these markings need not mean that we wrote them. I don't know who wrote them, and that was my answer of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Albanian?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looks like it was written by a Kosovo Albanian prisoner about another prisoner. And if we look at another one -- we'll take one for the 22nd. Perhaps just lay it straight on the overhead projector because I want to finish, if I may. I've got only one more question, I think, about this video and I'm done before the break, if the Court may possibly indulge me with a couple of minutes. Here one for another body, you see, which isn't the 23rd. This is the 22nd, if Mr. Nort can turn it round so we can see it. That's helpful. And again you see it has date, name, and it says "Dubrava." There's a format to the way these things are done. These show the dates upon which these people died, and one of them is the 23rd, and there are a couple more that are the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say again that I don't know what this refers to. However, have we not clearly shown with this that we worked according to the correct procedure and that we took note of every detail and that it is not part of a conspiracy for hiding the facts, as you put it, but that this is how things stood. I don't know what this refers to. I don't know who made this note, but the crime policemen took photographs of it as they found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, you have referred to Bojic's document dated the 22nd of May where he refers -- it's tab 46.3 -- where he refers to later reports that the bombing happened up to the 22nd of May at 6.10 in the morning. Even assuming the date of that report by the investigative judge is accurate, which I don't accept -- I don't accept. Even assuming it is, that couldn't possibly account for a killing on the 23rd when, as your own documents show, there was only overflying. Could it? And there is no --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What has that got to do with the killing?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what I'm going to suggest to you is that those who engaged in the wanton killing of many, many prisoners at Dubrava must have persuaded you and the other authorities to cover up their crime by trying to make it seem as if it was a later bombing that had done the damage. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand. However, the death of the prisoners was the result of the bombing. That is incontestable and can be seen from this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, incontestable. Thirty people with gunshots going through their heads, going straight through their bodies. That's caused by bombing, is it? And if so, would you like to explain what kind of bomb it is that lets off ordinary bullets? You see, we've got pathologist evidence on this, Mr. Paponjak. You may not have known that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of bullets?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bullets that come from guns. I haven't got the dimension of the bullet with me, but that's not an answer to the question. Can you tell me, please, what kind of bomb lets off bullets -- I think we've got one going through somebody's head, from here, down through his body and several other pictures of them going through -- I can give you the pictures, if you like. Would you like to see them? If you really think that would help you, and I don't want to go over the break, but I can show you the photographs, or some of them, of the evidence that we have in this case going to show how some of these people died.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have to defer this until after, but it will be the only thing I will defer until after apart from one part that I'd like to play straight away to the witness before we come to Baccard's evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just look at this bit of video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go back. That will do as well but just let's go back a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are the technicians, apparently, filming. Stop there. Did you see a gun in that technician's hand?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's a technician or a member of the security force or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears to be the group of people who have gone round photographing these bodies. You're a policeman. You were there at the time. You know the uniforms. Who were they? Police, special police, paramilitary? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you go back a bit and stop the film, maybe I can recognise them, but it would be nothing strange if the technicians or the others had guns in their hands. This last individual was probably a technician from the investigating team, and we were able to see a uniformed policeman a few seconds ago. The technicians are also authorised personnel from the Ministry of the Interior, for example, and it is not unusual for them to carry rifles in war situations because they can be attacked when arriving, when leaving, and on the spot itself as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are no weapons seen on the people taking the video on the 19th, were there? They were ordinary technicians. What's happened by this date?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were not recorded when getting out of vehicles. I don't think we have anything like that recorded. They must have had weapons on the vehicles that day, too, because it was quite customary and it was a normal thing for everybody to carry rifles as soon as they went out into the open, out of town, but also when they went to town too. There was a situation of war. There were attacks coming from all over, terrorists were everywhere. So it was quite natural for them to be armed with rifles, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See, what we see in this video is a video of people with mattresses in an area where they've been made to line up, been shot, where others had been pursued on that on subsequent days and attacked with grenades as they had been on the first day, and all the injuries that we can see on this video are consistent with that. Some killed in the bombing, some killed by things like grenades, and some shot. And that's my question to you, and answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Employees -- employees of the crime investigation police of the SUP of Pec carefully investigated this, carefully looked at this video footage. There is nothing on this footage that would indicate that these people had been shot, as you had put it. The conclusion that the experts reached on the basis of the available material is that this was a consequence of the NATO bombing and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to finish with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we're going to take the break now. This must be a convenient time. I think we are five minutes beyond. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, we've moved on from -- in the compilation video, from the part that had the men with guns at the car and the video of the bodies in the prison to the last part. It's on a freeze-frame at the moment, and you'll see that we're back to a version that has a date, 25th, and a time on it, and this is the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Sanction again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Sanction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this shows the bodies, one by one. You've produced this video. I want some help from you, please. First of all, to your knowledge was it all Kosovo Albanians who were buried on this occasion or were there any Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All who were found were buried there. All the corpses that were found, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were fingerprinted, weren't they, for the purposes of providing identification, because one of your reports shows that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's clear that there was, under your discrimination between times of anxiety when you might be worried about bombs coming and times of calm when you weren't, it's clear from this video that the video-takers were under no great pressure of time on the 25th. They're taking a very measured video. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was out in an open area that was not a target of aerial attacks, and that area was not expected to be targeted even if the planes were to fly over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made the decision not to examine the bodies for cause of death?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the bodies not being examined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've got -- oh, I see. Well, please, then, take us through your material and show us where is the analysis, documentarily recorded, body by body, showing of what they died.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the cause of death can be established only by carrying out a post-mortem, and there was no time for post-mortems or were there any possibilities for doing that because post-mortems were carried out in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, even if there wasn't time for full post-mortems, we can see from the photographs of the bodies their clothing wasn't even moved save for a few who had their trousers pulled down for some reason. Who made the decision not even to examine them sufficiently to discover whether, as was subsequently discovered in respect of 37 per cent of them, that they'd been shot?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision to carry out a post-mortem is always -- is always made by an investigating judge, according to our law. It's not that the law enforcement agencies decide on that. It was the investigating judge who examined the bodies and decided to have them buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his name or her name?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a record of the on-site investigation here, signed by Investigating Judge Vladan Bojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he was injured, of course, in the blast on the 19th or 21st -- 21st, I think. Who made the decision and where's -- where's the document that I can find that explains the decision-making process that led to these bodies being buried so quickly without any examination for cause of death?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although wounded, Investigating Judge Bojic went on carrying out his obligations, which is not the only case that this was done. All lightly wounded persons continued working. Only when hospitalisation was indispensable did a person not going on working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... decision? Where is the document that shows his decision? This is all your material, all these binders. You tell me where I can find it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2 of the record of the on-site investigation, which is among the documents here. That is tab 46. 46.1, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read that out to you if you haven't got it translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is the bit that explains everything? We've looked at parts of this document before, the flying over of planes and all that sort of thing, but where is the bit that explains his decision-making to have these bodies buried without inspection?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the investigation continued for the second time on the 25th of May, 1999, in the absence of elementary --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a specific reference in the document where this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have a specific reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 46.1 page 2 in the English, and it's towards the foot of the page, under the heading "Continuation of the on-site Investigation." You've got the files. Otherwise I can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was ordered was photographing the site and later on recording by video camera. "Then I ordered that all the killed persons be relocated from the site, and after getting out of the rubble, to be relocated to the Albanian cemetery in the village of Donja Susica, a few kilometres away from the site in the direction of Kosovska Mitrovica via Zubin Potok. After the relocation of all the corpses to the mentioned place, I ordered the photographing and fingerprinting of every corpse individually. At the same time, I ordered to have an external examination of all corpses, which was carried out by the physician M. Stijovic, a specialist surgeon employed in the general hospital in Pec. The entire process went on all the way until the 26th of May at 10.00."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A total of 93 bodies were taken out of the KPZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice stopped the witness when he was supposed to read out the last sentence only and that is relevant in terms of the question that was put. It reads as follows: "After carrying out all the ordered crime investigation procedures, I ordered to have the burial individual of bodies carried out in a legally prescribed way."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's on this second page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Paponjak, when people are trying to cover their traces, they sometimes say things that they shouldn't or fail to say things that they should. Here we see, I suggest to you, an example of that, because Mr. Bojic suggests indeed that there should be, in his report, should or should have been external examination of the bodies. Can you please show us on this video or in any of the records that you've produced that there was external examination of the bodies by Dr. Stijovic? Can you show it to us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why do you claim that he didn't have that carried out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the video. You've looked at it at great length. You explained to the Learned Judges how it would be a good idea for them to do the same. Here they are fully clothed save for a few. You can hear the earth mover in the background digging the graves. Where is there the evidence that these bodies were examined for cause of death? It's not on the video, and I'd like you, please, because there are so many untranslated documents, it may be there, to take me to Dr. Stijovic's reports that show the cause of death for these unfortunate people.
