utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in the documentation of the court of the investigating judge. We don't have that document because that document was not relevant for us at that point in time. Dr. M. Stijovic, specialist, submitted his report to the judge, not to the SUP Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what did it show -- or is this something where you can't help us because it's the responsibility of another ministry? What did it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. show for those 37 per cent of the victims who died from gunshot wounds? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean you don't have any such thing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the Secretariat of the Interior in Pec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it says here the whole process lasted until -- that's 1000 hours on 26 May this year. I'm interested to find out, to ascertain how long would that process of external examination have lasted if it started on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The video we are seeing now was taken on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in the afternoon. If the time there is right, it's in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would have been the examination of 93 bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help His Honour Judge Robinson, please, Mr. Paponjak, with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot because I really don't know about that. I was not present there all the time. I was there perhaps for half an hour only at the stage when the burial of the corpses had already started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that the burial of the bodies started within how long of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The burial was already under way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, did you see Dr. Stijovic there kitted out with a white or a green coat and rubber gloves, working in a tent or something like that, examining the bodies, did you, or did you just see the bodies put into the grave fully clothed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the spot itself I saw the bodies, I saw a tractor, or was it an earth mover that was used to dig the graves, and I saw a significant number of people there, perhaps about 15 of them. There was no tent there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I take up one point further?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last sentence of this tab, Mr. Paponjak, tab 46.1, says: "The forensic documentation represents an integral part of this record." What does it mean? Does it mean that Dr. Stijovic's report is included in this documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what it means. An investigating judge orders different participants to carry out particular actions. The forensic documentation, as it was called here, is what we have in the case file. That is what we have. The other participants who carry out certain activities submit their report to the investigating judge, not to us. We are only part of the team on site that is carrying out investigation activities. There are experts engaged by the investigating judge who submit their reports to him. We don't have the reports of Dr. Stijovic for those reasons, and perhaps some other reports that the investigating judge has. What is contained here is only what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to understand that while you are able to bring here the record of on-site investigation written by Judge Bojic that you are not able to bring here the very important report of Dr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigating judge usually submits his record to us. In some cases, it so happened because we have records of judgements, we also have the actual texts of the decisions, but we don't have the other documentation. They don't submit that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Paponjak, you were there early on -- by the way, what was a traffic policeman, if you were a traffic policeman, doing at an event like this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean what he did?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a traffic policeman. What were you doing at a scene of crime investigation and burial of this importance? Was there a lot of traffic to direct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't a lot of traffic, but it's right by the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you on patrol and you just happened to sort of pop in to the grave site or were you there for a purpose?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was there for a purpose, of course, but I wasn't on patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was the purpose of the traffic inspector being there? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific task in this respect, no specific job. I just stopped by for a brief period of time to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just out of interest, to see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any specific assignment in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the first time when you went there? Was it on the 19th? Did you have any job then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, no specific assignment. The bombing was on. Those of us who happened to be there heard about it and went to the site itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, if we go back to your answers when I asked you about what happened on arrival and what you saw and you described the bodies, the tractor and the burial, if I asked you the question, "From your own knowledge, from your own observations was there any external examination of the bodies that you saw," your answer would be?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I seen it? The answer would have been that I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, can I clarify something? It may be me that has misunderstood earlier evidence. What exactly was your position in the office in Pec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Pec I was head of the department of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That does clarify it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I return, with that question and answer in mind, to an earlier topic, and then I am completely done. You will remember that I suggested to you that you were much more implicated in events than you revealed, possibly in relation to the Salihaj family, and certainly in relation to the movement of the bodies from Batajnica. I want you to have a few more details to consider about the movement of bodies. First, did you know and is it right that the movement of bodies was aimed at avoiding the detection of crimes? No bodies; no crimes. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that that's what you're asking me. However, that is not something that I knew, and it's not correct anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm going to suggest to you, and let me make it clear this will emerge within a couple of months, in my suggestion, in a public report, so think carefully: Were you aware that bodies from Pec were found in sites 3 and 5 at Batajnica as long ago as 2002?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain? Will you let me explain what I knew about that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some kind of removal of bodies was referred to in the newspapers. From the newspapers and from television, I found out that allegedly these bodies were found. Now, when was that? It was in that year. And nothing else. We did not receive any information about this, let alone that it was bodies from Pec that were found there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between December of last year and April of this year, Judge Dilparic has been the investigative judge dealing with this, and so far more than 50 bodies from those Batajnica sites have now been identified as coming from Pec. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a certain amount of information that some bodies had been identified and that they were handed over at the checkpoint to families from Kosovo and Metohija. That is true, and that is contained in our documentation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it must be my mistake, but let me see if I follow this. You're now acknowledging, because I've mentioned the investigative judge, that you were aware that Pec bodies had been found in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That pertains to what you asked about, December last year. The first question was 2002 or, rather, 1999, or whatever the year you mentioned was. I'm giving you a precise answer to the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while you've been sitting there, you have at all times known that bodies from Pec had been identified as found in Batajnica and indeed had been returned to their original Pec family members. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are not bodies from Pec. These were identified persons from the area of Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Identified persons from the area of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you questions earlier this morning, and we'll try and find the precise answers you gave so that you can consider them, did you not think that I might have been referring to bodies from the area of Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now it seems that on the basis that a person was identified who had resided in Pec, that this body was transferred from Pec itself. I don't know what you meant. I told you quite specifically that we received information that bodies that were identified as being bodies of former residents of Pec were returned so that they could be buried properly. But that does not mean that they were found in Pec and transported from there. They could have arrived from other places too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you questions earlier this morning about movement of bodies from Pec to Batajnica - we may not be able in the time to find the quotes - but you made it clear that you knew absolutely nothing about this, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely nothing about any removals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you now tell us that you knew about the return of the bodies, may we take it that your first answer was inevitably some form of lie?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot convince anyone of that. Those two have nothing to do with each other. I know nothing about the relocation of bodies, but I do know that some bodies were returned. They were found somewhere, they were identified as being those bodies, and they were returned. Again, that has nothing to do with their movement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me help you just with a few of your answers about bodies from Pec to Batajnica. You challenged me, saying, "While you're at it, you can say I dug them up personally. Nothing like that happened, and I didn't participate in it." And later you said, "I cannot say anything of that sort," when I suggested to you that you'd been involved, "because it didn't happen. I didn't know anything about it. Even less could I say that I participated in it myself." You were trying to mislead this Court --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been trying to mislead this Court and you've been caught out because I presented you with the evidence you didn't think I would have, namely that the investigating judge has already reported to you on bodies moving from Pec to Batajnica. You've been caught out, Mr. Paponjak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I also remind you that you had said that, I quote, "We did not receive any information about this, let alone that it was bodies from Pec that were found there."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We were talking about bodies that had been transferred from Pec. To date, no such information exists. It was announced in public that the bodies had been returned to families. And the Prosecutor cannot allege that I said I didn't know about it. However, we have no information that bodies had been dug out from cemeteries and transferred to Serbia. We have some information that some bodies were identified and returned to families. There is no link with reburial. It doesn't mean that those bodies had been buried in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is what I understand the witness to be saying, that while there may be evidence that bodies were found in Batajnica and returned to families in Pec, there is no evidence that those bodies were removed from Pec, dug up from Pec and taken to Batajnica. That's what I understand him to be saying. That's understandable. Just to correct something in the transcript. When you said to the witness, "You are trying to mislead this Court," the transcript has the witness as answering "That's right," but to be fair to him, you had not finished the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak, His Honour explains that your answer is comprehensible or capable of being comprehended, but I'm going to suggest to you that your answer is nonsense. Perhaps you'd like to explain, please, how bodies killed in the course of the events between March and June of 1999 got themselves up to the air force base in Batajnica near Belgrade so as to be buried along with other bodies that had been dug up in various parts of Kosovo and transferred to hide the evidence? Can you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That still doesn't mean they were dug up in Pec --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they dug up?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as you tried to put in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they dug up?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back and give you a last chance to think about this. Amongst other sources of information, forensic scientific, there's your fellow policeman Zoran Aleksic, who was driven away because he was prepared to tell the truth about you and your colleagues. Do you want to think again about whether you along with Vlahovic, Bulatovic, Milojevic Mladen and Zoran Stanisic were involved in this? Do you want to think again about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need to think about something I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you again that I did not participate in that, even if it happened, nor do I know of such a thing happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be quite clear, the role of the traffic police in the event, amongst others, was that they were engaged in identifying the corpse -- corpses to be moved by gender and age, it being part of the plan to leave behind bodies that were KLA and to take away bodies that were innocent victims. Do you follow me? That's the suggestion as to what you and your particular group of police were doing.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is simply ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Than you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have re-examination, Mr. Robinson. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you are going to re-examine, I want a disciplined exercise re-examination. It's confined to matters arising from the cross-examination. No leading questions, and it must be of a reasonably -- a reasonable length.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I should have made this point clear before sitting down: As to the exhibits, although as I indicated I would ask questions about them without prejudice to their admissibility, it will be my argument in due course that the evidence given by this witness shows that the documents should not be admitted. He has no sufficient firsthand knowledge of the details he's referring to. He's relied entirely on the unidentified authorship of others. He's never been able to give detailed answers when asked, and this falls below the level of evidence acceptability set by this Chamber. I thought I ought to make that clear before re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, to reply to what Mr. Nice just said, Colonel, when you said on several occasions that you had not written the documents that you had signed, when you said you had not written them, did you say that in order to explain that you cannot know every detail by heart or to say that you cannot stand by those documents and their authenticity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prepared those documents together, I mean the team that prepared them, and I participated in the preparation of this underlying information. I didn't mean to say that I don't stand by those documents. I stand by every document because it was the work product of a team of which I was a part, so I do absolutely stand by each of these documents because it is the result of joint work, and I signed them, of course, as head of Secretariat of the Interior. Some of the examinations were not performed by me, which is only natural. Many incidents were processed by forensic policemen and scene-of-crime officers, but we had the documents available when we prepared these reports. I did review certain case files in which I was personally interested in, or professionally interested in, and I know the details, but there were other cases which were not the subject of my professional interest, and I had no opportunity to explain this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm giving you this opportunity now. So all these case files that now exist in the relocated Secretariat of the Interior of Pec were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prepared under your leadership?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all the documents, did all the underlying documents pass through your hands and the hands of your associates who participated in the preparation of these documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them even contain my handwritten notes in the margin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just complete this. On whose orders did you prepare these briefs or information that were prepared in the Secretariat of the Interior in Pec and in Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice suggested that you prepared this in order to help me. Who headed the Ministry of the Interior when you received those orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dusan Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice mentioned here that some people have already testified here. Did your Secretariat of the Interior follow the evidence given in this trial?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not check that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that since you received the assignment to prepare this you were also provided with the methodology and the required headings. Those people who gave you orders to prepare these documents, are they the same people who sent me here?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that seems to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we then assume that those people wanted you to do something to help me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no grounds for such an assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, look at this: A subject of considerable examination by Mr. Nice was tab 2.4, "Information about the forcible deportation of Albanians, their persecution, and acception [as interpreted] of IDs and personal documents." Was that one of the headings that were given to you by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that the reason why it was included, as one of the required headings according to the orders of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We could not change that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this attachment, which is mentioned in para 7 and refers to one of the counts in the indictment, means that you had the task of compiling all the information about deportations, the taking away of IDs, et cetera, to respond to these charges?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were not doing it to help me but, rather, to help Mr. Nice in order to prove his case?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way I understood it, but it can be understood differently as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if it is required to compile all information about deportations of Albanians on ethnic and racial grounds, et cetera, et cetera, did you give orders to your team to gather all the information related to deportations of Albanians, persecution on ethnic and racial grounds, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your conclusion? Is your conclusion reflected in the sentence that says "This information is not correct"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate what the interpreters are telling me, that I have to make a pause between question and answer. Is it then clear that your assignment was to provide information concerning cases in which Albanians were the injured party and that you did precisely what you were asked?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you required, and we have documents here from which we can see that, such as one document in particular which refers exclusively to cases where Albanians were victimised, were you required by the Ministry of the Interior to provide information first about those cases where Albanians were the injured party? Was priority given to Albanians or Serbs, Roma, and others?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were asked as a priority to provide this information concerning Albanians and later concerning cases involving Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later, when you were required to provide information about forcible deportations and persecution of Albanians, you were also required to provide information about crimes against Albanians.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not required to provide information about crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was it before you were required to provide information on crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considerably later. I cannot tell you exactly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it after you completed compiling information on crimes against Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice asked you in particular about one brief which concerns security related events involving loss of life from the 1st of January, 1998, until the 1st of June, 2001, in tab 4. He only asked you about item 59, which you quoted in its entirety, and there's no need for me to read it again. I suppose you well remember that it concerns a summary. I'll quote only one part, which says, "Members of the police responded to fire." That follows after the sentence about the attack on the police patrol. It also mentions that eight KLA members were killed, quoting names. Mr. Nice asked at one point -- in fact, he claimed that those people had their throats slit. Do you know anything about that, and is there any information that reality is different from this summary?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What throats? What throats were slit? That is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this entire file A/III, item 59, has a case file behind it for every item, including 59?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have case files numbered including lists of victims in alphabetical order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the underlying information that we used for this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for this entire documentation that you exhibited here, there are underlying dossiers and case files for every incident, every case.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that each of these documents under each of these tabs is an official document of the Ministry of the Interior, officially signed and stamped, together with all the underlying case files?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. We couldn't work any different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I will ask you to exhibit these documents, especially if we have in mind that Mr. Nice is exhibiting documents from secondhand, fifth-hand sources such as books including "Under Orders" which have no evidentiary value at all. We are talking here, on the contrary, about official documents and forensic documentation obtained during investigations. So if you make any comparison in terms of validity between various documents tendered here, you must bear in mind, of course, that official documents certainly have priority over the documents provided by Mr. Nice, especially documents provided by BBC, including their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Paponjak, where do you come from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you say? Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are from Rudo. And I am from Pozarevac. And now look, in this document that Mr. Nice tried to explain to you in the Serbian language, and that is document military district Pec, which says "moving part of the population from the zone of responsibility," does that mean population that is native to that area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people here know the Serbian language better than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's clear that if they were to relocate, they were to be relocated outside this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tend to forecast leading questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll allow him to finish. Finish the question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This first sentence here, does it read: "Moving out part of the population from the zone of responsibility of VO Pec, military district Pec," and then goes on to say, "with a view to proper functioning and normal life in the zone of responsibility." Let me not ask a leading question: What does this mean, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means what I tried to explain when asked by Mr. Nice, by the Prosecutor: This was to regulate the relocation of the population from those places where their lives could have been in jeopardy, such as positions of the army or the police to a different location that is safer. That is all there is to it. This is not about deportation or moving out, it's about relocation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Is the purpose of this measure to protect population or to deport it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are protective measures that are applied by all military units expecting to come under attack, expecting to be involved in combat activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I hope we've clarified this. Now, let us shed light on some of the other issues raised by Mr. Nice regarding the Dubrava prison. Mr. Nice mentioned tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just give us that tab number again, the one which deals with moving out of or moving from or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 319, tab 36.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the tab number, Mr. Robinson. This is something that was introduced by Mr. Nice in cross-examination. That is his exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exhibit 319, tab 36. I'm going to ask that it be passed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich provided him with a copy, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that it be translated, that the interpreters translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the Philip Coo binder, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We have single versions of it for ease of handling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to have a Serb version placed on the ELMO so that the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't happen to have Mr. Coo's exhibit bundles in my pocket, which I remember were very extensive. I wonder if there are English language versions, that they could be distributed to Your Honours and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we had an English language version this morning. That's the problem. It's suggested that the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't mind seeing that as well so that we can bear it in mind, if it can be distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have in front of me both what I just read out from a Serbian text when I was examining the colonel, and I have the English translation that was provided together with this when Mr. Nice tendered it. The English translation is incorrect. Instead of saying that this population -- it says -- [In English] "Moving of a part of the population out of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I know you're gifted linguistically, but I'd prefer to have it placed on the ELMO so that it can be translated. Could you pass over the Serbian version. Put it on the ELMO, and we'll ask the interpreters to translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. May I just ask the interpreters something, because as expert, they can testify, too, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want any evidence on it, Mr. Milosevic. Just let the interpreters translate what they say. What paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the second sentence at the very beginning: "Moving part of the population from the zone of responsibility." Would you please lower it a little. [In English] Down, down. Just the opposite direction. [Interpretation] No, scroll it up a bit. That's it. You see here the second sentence says: "And moving or relocating part of the population from the zone of responsibility of the military district of Pec with a view to proper functioning of the entire life in the zone of responsibility of the Pec military district." Whereas the translation says "moving out."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I want you to be quiet. Let the interpreters do this translation for me again. The interpreters, please. Just read the text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From which part, Your Honour? Where do we start? Somebody should read it for us to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can't you see what is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From the beginning, it reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- "First command of the military section of Pec, strictly confidential."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can skip that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sub-heading "Functioning of life and order."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Skip that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "Pursuant to the order of the Supreme Commander proclaiming the state of war and the relocation of a part of a population from the zone of responsibility of the Pec military district with a view to proper functioning of the entire life in the zone of responsibility of the Pec military district, I hereby order..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is all. So this interpreter interpreted this correctly. It should read in translation "from the zone," whereas the document provided by Mr. Nice says "part of the population out of the zone." That is not a possible translation. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She also said "relocation," which has some significance too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well except -- well, okay. I'm afraid I remain subject to the same problem as I had before, that "from the zone" is, as I understand it, exactly the same "out of the zone." I don't see the difference unless there's some particular word in Serbian in this context where "from" means "of," the population of the zone. But to relocate a part of a population from a zone simply means to me out of the zone, but it may be a problem of translation that is extremely difficult to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I asked the witness precisely for this purpose, "Where are you from, Mr. Paponjak?" And he answered, "From Rudo." In the Serbian language, you say, "I come from this and that place," just like you said "from the zone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, people say that in English also, that I would be from Scotland. I understand that entirely. But I would never talk about the population "from" Scotland. I would always talk about the population "of" Scotland, and that's where I have the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the reference here is to two words that were mistranslated. The reference in the original is to relocation, which was mistranslated as "moving out." And it further says "out of the zone." Those two combined change the sense completely. The witness, however, explained exactly what this was all about. I asked the witness what the purpose was, protection or maltreatment, and he answered protection. Of course, this was always the main purpose, to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no difficulty accepting that the correct translation of the word is "from," but it remains a matter of interpretation now what that whole sentence actually means, and that's for us to deal with at an appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, Mr. Nice mentioned tab 7. In tab 7, there is a brief about the consequences of NATO bombing in the area of responsibility of Pec. I don't have to read the entire document, because it pertains to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entire period of aggression. Tab 7 contains the documents as they occurred chronologically from item 64 onwards. Istok, Dubrava. Then the 19th of May from 8.20 until 10.20. And then there is the actual case reference and everything else. Then you come to point 60, Istok Dubrava, the 21st of May, paragraph 65, and then the times are given.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we come to 66. Yes, 66. Istok Dubrava, the 21st of May at 17.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then it goes on case file, et cetera. And the people killed are mentioned in all cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I don't know whether the Chamber wants to be sensitive to this: I didn't cross-examine on this document, I think, at all, not least because I didn't have a translation of it. I cross-examined and asked a few questions about tab 8, but I didn't cross-examine about tab 7. Indeed, if it had been translated I might have wanted to do so, but I didn't have it, and I didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us hear the question so we can determine whether to allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that you will recall well that Mr. Nice insisted several times upon the times when the prison was bombed in his cross-examination, all the times. And now I have pulled out tab 7, and I do remember him mentioning tab 7. But if he didn't read it, I accept that. But it is legitimate, because he asked questions about the times of the bombings of the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tab 7 doesn't have any times on it. Is it tab 7.1 perhaps, or 7.2, or some later one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's 7.2, I think. And it's very -- this is a real good example of how not having translated documents is problematic. Of course I can see, looking at them now, that various dates related to Istok Dubrava are referred to, didn't form part of the accused's evidence in chief, and in the absence of an English version to deal with, I didn't prepare on the basis of it. So there it is. I don't know whether when I see an English version there would be any points I would have wanted to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But it would arise. Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in tab 7, point 64 is Dubrava prison from 8.20 to 10.20. Then 65, once again Dubrava on the 25th of May from 0830 hours to 1030 hours. Point 66, Dubrava, the 21st of May, around 1750 hours. That's 66. Then we come to 67 chronologically, Pec, Branovacko Brdo [phoen], which has nothing to do with Dubrava, but already when we come to point 68, we have Istok Dubrava the 21st of May from 2340 to 2345 hours. Then we come to 69, Istok Dubrava, the 22nd of May from 1300 hours to 1500 hours. And those are all -- that is to say, from 64 to 69 inclusive, we have all the events, all the instances of bombing of Dubrava prison with the exception of point 67, which was inserted there chronologically between 66 and 68 but does not refer to the Dubrava prison. Now, Colonel, is this the customary and usual way or normal phrases that are used, the customary phrases, if I can put it that way? But let's clear one point up first: On different days sometimes more people were killed, sometimes less people were killed by the bombing. It wasn't that when the bombing took place and we have recorded, as we have seen from point 69 -- 64 to 69 inclusive - how many does that make? - five or six instances of bombing, not the same number of people died on all the bombings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you notice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. One that's out with the area that we've looked at already is number 69. Now, what does it -- what does it actually say, Mr. Paponjak? What does the report number 69 say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'd better hold on. I'm getting no translation for this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Start again, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bombing of the Dubrava correctional centre with a number of projectiles, persons were killed, several persons were killed, wounded seriously or less seriously, and material damage was done to the prison. A report was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. In the three days of bombing 100 persons were killed and another 140 persons were wounded seriously or less seriously. An on-site investigation was carried out by the investigating judge from the district court of Pec with cooperation from the employees of the SUP of Pec. Crime and technical documents were compiled, a scene of the crime recorded and video footage made and an Official Note compiled. Sixty-seven bodies were fingerprinted for identification purposes. Twenty-six of the bodies were not fingerprinted because of the decomposition of the bodies. The corpses were buried individually pursuant to the laws and regulations. Video attachments 1/X, 2/X, 3/X, 4/X and 1/XI. So those are the partial videotapes per day of the bodies. And the case number is J/369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not actually say what happened between 1300 and 1500 hours on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What does it say happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the beginning it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the title, under number 69. "Istok Dubrava, the 22nd of May, between 1300 and 1500 hours."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but what does it say happened? What you read was the bombing of the Dubrava correctional centre with a number of projectiles, persons were killed, several persons were killed, wounded seriously or less seriously, and material damage was done to the prison. A report was sent to the ministry. In the three days of bombing, 100 persons were killed. What I'm trying to find out is what it says actually happened between 1300 and 1500 hours on the 22nd of May, and it would appear it doesn't deal with that. Now, can you clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this, I can't clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, these first few lines, do they refer to that day the 22nd of May between 1300 and 1500 hours? That is to say that the penal and correctional facility was -- of Dubrava was bombed, et cetera, with several projectiles and that the report sent to Serbian MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is no way to conduct a re-examination. The witness has already dealt with a question put in an open way by me and says he can't explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, looking -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but looking at the answer of the witness and trying to compare what one can track from the translation to the original by reference to numbers which we can all follow, he volunteered an observation about partial videotapes per day of the bodies which I suspect does not appear in the text, and this is clearly a document and may be a document I would have wanted to ask questions about in light of the material we have been supplied with and, of course, in light of the answers that the witness has himself given about the impossibility of there being a video, an on-site investigation on the 22nd. Because you'll remember that's one of the days when they were all too frightened to go, and yet here there appears to be one. So there's a lot of material that should have been available to us in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, in all of this, in all these points, from 64, 5, 8, 9, and so on, do we find the same terms used and the same phrase, "the bombing of the penal and correctional facility of Dubrava," et cetera, et cetera, and then "several persons were killed, wounded," et cetera? Are the first three sentences or phrases the same? When it says that several -- a number of persons were killed, were wounded either seriously or less seriously, it's the same phrase, the same turn of phrase used in all these points for the Dubrava prison, although we have actually established that at some time -- that sometimes more persons were killed, sometimes less. So how come these same phrases were used in all the cases? What is the official terminology that you used to express things like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, so many leading questions in that last effort from you. One doesn't know where it is leading to. The last question is: What is the official terminology used to express things like this? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I'd like to answer the comment made by the Prosecutor. Everything that was added subsequently, after saying that a report was sent to the MUP of Serbia, relates to our collective knowledge gathered about each particular event, because that is the latest report on the bombing which is a compilation of all the knowledge we had. That is why it contains information about fingerprinting, videotaping, and all the rest of it. So this is the last time that the bombing was mentioned, and it mentions the consequences of the bombings, all the consequences. I understood the Prosecutor to say that there was an on-site investigation and these were attachments on the basis of that. An on-site investigation wasn't conducted on that day but the video attachments 1/10 to 4/10 and 1/11 are the complete tapes to be found in the files on that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, in point 69, para 69, the first four lines, do those refer to the event that took place on the 22nd of May? Is that a standard form?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is standard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas all the rest refers to the cumulative information gathered, that particular case and the previous ones. Can that be seen from the text? That's what I wanted to clear up.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you yourself said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll stop here now and take the break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a look at all these items, from 65 to 69, with the exception of 67, which does not pertain to Dubrava? The same sentence was used time and again: "Several persons were killed or -- and sustained serious and less serious injuries."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a general formulation that was used because the exact number was not established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wanted to establish. So there is no difference in this description of events from day to day. The same sentence is used every time, that is to say, "Several persons," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, because it was not known how many. And then finally there is paragraph 69, which brings all of this together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know whether all facilities of the Dubrava prison were hit during these airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a single facility within it that was not hit during the aerial strikes?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at that time there were over 1.000 convicts or accused persons there; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there was a total of 1.004 detainees or prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a facility where there are 1.004 detainees, if all facilities within that compound were hit, is it reasonable to expect that -- about this many to be killed or wounded? That's less than 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's leading. That has to be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the facilities within the compound were hit, and there is a total of 1.004 prisoners there. Ninety-five of them were killed. Are those the facts that were established?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Those are the facts that were established. Ninety-seven killed persons, or perhaps a bit more, I can't say just off-the-cuff now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice showed the dining area where there are no corpses, and before that did you notice a part of the dining area where there were several corpses, before that on the tape?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is such footing on the tape as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a bomb fell in through the ceiling of the dining area, would it jettison the corpses away from that spot?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is only logical that they would be killed and that the bodies would be thrown elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 46.5 - there wasn't any need to translate this because it was taken out of the white book - is there -- are there some photographs there from the prison of Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me just try to find this. I'm afraid that this is not it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 46.5. That's where the photographs are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I place these photographs on the ELMO now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you pass it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to place on the overhead projector some of these. You don't have to put all of them on. From 322 onwards, just briefly. From page 322 onwards. But that's not it. Now we've got the photographs. Next, please. Next, please. These are the effects of the air bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is this in relation to? You are not at large in re-examination. What does it arise from? If you can't establish that, I will not allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to Mr. Nice's question. He put not only one question but many questions as to whether post-mortems were carried out in order to establish how persons got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we have the next photograph, please, in relation to the question put in cross-examination by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic, and what do these photographs have to do with that question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, if you'd please look at the next photograph, you'd see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have to explain to me how the question which you're asking relates to an issue that arises from cross-examination. I'm waiting for the explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the next photographs, you can see quite clearly that there are several corpses there, on the one down here and the next ones, where people obviously got killed in the bombing. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but how does that relate to any issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It relates to the questions put by Mr. Nice in relation to the doctor who examined the corpses, and he asked whether post-mortems were carried out, examinations, et cetera. My question is related to that question put by Mr. Nice; whether the authorities there, where it was quite clear how a person found his or her death, do they carry out post-mortems nevertheless? Please look at the next photograph. If a person is taken out of rubble after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can ask the question, but we don't need the assistance of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may -- incidentally, been looking at the photographs and the accused may be confused and it would be unfortunate to confuse anyone else. These all relate to the 19th of May. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They can be matched to the film and there is no challenges to that they died or how they died.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we want to establish exactly what this pertains to, it pertains to the 19th and 21st of May. On page 319, that is at the beginning of tab 46.5, it says that 95 persons were killed and 196 were wounded. That is the information contained at the very beginning. It pertains to the 19th and 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Colonel, during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you ask, are you telling us that any of these pictures relate to a period other than the 19th of May? That's the photographs in particular. Are you saying that any one of these relates to later than the 19th of May? That's the pictures of bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I cannot say specifically which date these photographs pertain to, but at the very outset, at the beginning of this document that was published as the white book, from page 319 onwards there is reference to the 19th and 21st of May. Now, what pertains to the 19th and what pertains to the 21st or some other day is something that I cannot say. But obviously these pictures were taken in the prison in the immediate aftermath of the bombing, and you can see how many persons were hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has made the point that you can tell from the video shot after the 19th of May that these bodies relate to the 19th of May. Now, do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is all on the tape from the 19th and the 21st of May, and everything else is on the tape, too, pertaining to other dates. The tape is an exhibit, and it's from the investigation that was carried out, and I cannot just say off the top of my head which body pertains to which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be that photograph 4 relates to the 21st, I'll get the copy of the white book and examine it, but as to the bodies, Your Honours' understanding of my position is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a very simple question: In this brief concerning the effects of the NATO bombing, you gave a series of cases, 97 cases of bombing in the area of responsibility of your Secretariat of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wherever there were casualties in these events, and when this was established immediately after the bombing, was a special investigation carried out or were post-mortems carried out, or was it obvious how these people had lost their lives? Was it customary for post-mortems to be carried out in case of bombing victims?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't customary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I said that it's for the investigating judge to decide whether a post-mortem would be carried out or not. It was probably obvious to the investigating judge why -- how this was done, and therefore there was no reason for this to be carried out. Also, in those situations it was virtually impossible to carry out a post-mortem. It was virtually impossible to find a forensic doctor who would carry that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Paponjak - excuse me - do you happen to know when this white book was published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date, but I think it was published sometime in 2003 or somewhere around there. I'm just saying this off-the-cuff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The white book was published in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've got it here. You've got the white book here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why this does not say the bombing on the 22nd, on page 319.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I did not participate in the elaboration of this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions in relation to Dubrava. You were asked whether there was any military target within the compound and in the immediate vicinity of the prison.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that question was put to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any military facility or any military piece of equipment or vehicle, an APC, a truck that was destroyed in the prison or near the prison during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There weren't any military facilities or military equipment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Nice asked you about tab 9, too, which is a very voluminous piece of information. 9 and 9.1. 9 is the text, and then the entire list is 9.1. That is a detailed piece of information about the terrorist organisation and the terrorist activities. That's contained in the heading "Information about terrorist organisation and terrorist activities and the effects of terrorist activities carried out by the KLA in the territory of the SUP of Pec." He put a question to you, to read the first paragraph on page 1. "Albanian separatism and extremism in the previous period" is the sub-heading and then he asked you why you needed 1878 [as interpreted] and the Prizren League and all the rest of that in the first paragraph. Colonel, as far as I can see, this entire history, including the Second World War, ends by the middle of the first page, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These few lines at the very beginning, were they given by way of historical background for further developments or in order to describe something, or was it intended to be some kind of historical text?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done so that whoever would read it would find his way and know more about it. There was no other reason. This information was compiled for our own purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the purposes of the police with a historical background of events, and very quickly they move on to the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question about the parapolice, which starts from the middle of page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document that particularly interested and concerned me but which there was simply not time to get a translation. I was indeed hoping, had time moved more swiftly -- time moved more slowly and I moved more swiftly this morning, to have returned to it if I could have found passages. However, I only cross-examined in the event on the opening passage, and it is completely unsatisfactory for a document of this kind to be examined item by item without the Court having the complete document to look at. I know from those who have reviewed it what my general propositions about this document would be, and the Court will need to look at it in -- as a whole, given both the single question I was able to ask and, I think, the single question that came from the Bench yesterday, to see if there is any value in the re-examination now intended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have some sympathy for the Prosecutor's submissions, but let me hear first, what is it that you're seeking to establish?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this examination, I wish to refute Mr. Nice's claim that this is irrelevant. He wanted to diminish the value of this document, which is a very comprehensive and detailed overview of terrorist activity in the area of the Secretariat of the Interior of Pec from the 1st of January 1998 to the 1st of June, 2001, as we can see from the heading. And the very fact that the first few sentences provide a historical background was used by Mr. Nice to diminish the value of a document which contains a wealth of good information. This is a typical attempt to treat condescendingly documents which could be valuable exhibits by saying simply that this is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you never used this document in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was used by Mr. Nice in cross-examination with a view to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He only used the first -- number 1, the first part, which has to do with history, and you're now seeking to utilise the rest of the document, which in any event is not translated. I will consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll not allow it. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with Dubrava, just a few more questions, please. You mentioned that you did go to that cemetery in Rakos where Dubrava inmates were buried.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a cemetery even before the inmates were buried there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a Muslim cemetery in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the case that during the war other persons were buried there, persons who got killed in combat and generally during the conflict that took place in the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that some bodies were dug out from their graves there, bodies that had the marks of bullet wounds. Did those bodies include some of persons who died from being shot?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you why the burial was so hurried, and we have here a document prepared by the investigating judge who ordered the burial. Was there a danger of contamination, of contagion involved during those days? Was the burial indeed hasty?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was done in the only way possible. The bodies were already undergoing changes due to decomposition. They were decaying, and that was the only reason why it made no sense to delay their burial. But they were not buried before proper procedure was observed and every action prescribed by the law taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any omission made in that procedure, including fingerprinting, examination, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no omission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will no longer come back to these photographs. Mr. Nice further asked you why, after relocating to Kragujevac, you continued to work on the gathering of information concerning these crimes. He said verbatim, and I noted it, "Since you knew you were not coming back ..." Do you know that according to Resolution 1214 it was envisaged that our army and police should return immediately after takeover by the KFOR? Immediately, not several years later?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And to this date, I'm not sure that we are not going back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice asked you whether anyone, anyone from the outside, and he even mentioned Bosnia, whether anyone trained people from Pec. Do you have any knowledge that anyone from Pec had gone for some training in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that any policemen, and you knew all the policemen, ever attended some training in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you to tell us your opinion on the allegations of the president of Human Rights Watch from Pec, and according to what we saw from the ELMO, I read the name. It was Mr. Demaj. Did you ever hear of a person called Demaj who was president of the Human Rights Watch from Pec?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know no such person. And by the way, what he said there he could have said in Pec, and he could have reported everything to the police if he had anything to report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Mr. Nice insists that the work of Human Rights Watch is public, is it possible that the activity of Mr. Demaj is public, that he is president of Human Rights Watch in Pec while you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not possible. If there were any abuses by the police, then he could have come straight to us and reported. He could have reported it to any commanding officer. If there was anything happening that was out of order, it would have been logical to report it to me or the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice presented several allegations of maltreatment of Albanians by the police. You told us that since Pec is a small town, the citizens knew all the policemen working in Pec.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it then be logical to expect this president of Human Rights Watch, if he's talking about police abuse, to state the name of the policeman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your questions are provocatively leading. I believe that you know that you are leading. "Would it then be logical..." We have been through this before. You're telling the witness the answer to the question. It's abusive, and you must desist, otherwise, I'll stop the re-examination. If you're not able to ask questions which are not leading, then it means that you're not competent to carry out the re-examination. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice also claimed, basing himself on information provided by Human Rights Watch, that in 1993 there were some paramilitary groups in Pec. Do you know anything, anything at all about any paramilitary group in Pec in 1993 or around that year?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such thing, and I don't know anything about it. There were no paramilitary groups in the context in which the question was asked. It's possible that there were some paramilitary groups up in the mountains, in Cicavica and such like where terrorists were being trained, but there were no Serb paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what Mr. Nice quoted from reports of the Human Rights Watch, there seem to have been allegations about a paramilitary group in Pec even owning a barracks.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not possible. That's preposterous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it have been possible for a paramilitary group to exist in Pec and even have a barracks without you knowing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's simply impossible. Anyway, the person who made this allegation could have designated the barracks involved. Just throwing this allegation about without specifying the barracks makes no sense. I have said several times today if there was any police abuse by a specific policeman - and a case was mentioned today of a policeman who requisitioned some buses - then it would have been normal to say exactly who it was, and the policeman must have issued some papers in exchange for these buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice also quoted this gentleman from Human Rights Watch saying that police took money from shop owners in Pec. Do you know of a single case wherein the police in Pec took money from shop owners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. If money was taken from some shop owners, then the representative of this organisation could have stated which policeman did that by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said in cross-examination that people were arrested because they assembled in order to talk, to discuss. Do you know of a single case when, let us say an Albanian because in this case we are discussing mostly Albanians, do you know of a single case where an Albanian was arrested because a group had assembled to talk?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If that had been the practice, then the entire town of Pec would have been under arrest, because everybody gathered to talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice mentioned a lawyer, Adem Bajri, from Pec, who, as he said, defended 200 political prisoners starting with 1990. Do you know of any political prisoners in Pec from the time when you arrived there in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't even know what the term "political prisoner" means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a small misunderstanding at one point here, and Mr. Bonomy told me to pick that issue in re-examination. Namely, Mr. Nice asked you with regard to the illegal SUP whether you knew that your colleagues, Albanian policemen, members of the illegal SUP, had been arrested. Were any of these people who were members of the illegal SUP your colleagues at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that anyone was my colleague if he was a member of the so-called illegal SUP or illegal MUP of the Republic of Kosovo.
