They would come to perform an on-site investigation after we performed ours, and in some cases they even arrived before we did, and they conducted examinations. That almost always happened in situations where Albanians were involved. They never conducted an on-site investigation where Serbs were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know any of the policemen who had been regular policemen before in the SUP of Pec and who were later arrested as members of the illegal SUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have all the information about all the people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. arrested, but there was a story circulating that Serif Shala had been arrested. He first worked as a regular policeman in the SUP of Pec before leaving the service, and he was one of those who were arrested as illegal SUP members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone from the regular SUP of Pec who was arrested later as a member of this illegal MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know there was a trial, but I don't know about the outcome because I didn't follow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nice showed us yesterday on the ELMO a document that wasn't distributed, by the way, which he said was a report by some military source, a military document concerning the 25th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was an existing Prosecution exhibit, as the accused will recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that in this document -- in fact, Mr. Nice said it was a military document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May 1998 in Kosovo, were there any military missions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were probably some foreign military missions. Did you notice that it is written in this document that they had stated -- that's exactly what it says, I noted it, that term was used -- the people they found there told them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what they say. Did you notice that there was a description of a man wearing ammunition belts for a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who carried ammunition and who was armed at the time? Was it the KLA or civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a matter of course that it was not civilians. Who is armed? It's the KLA and the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we in fact see from this document that it was the KLA who told something to this mission?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see from the description that this mission learnt about something from KLA members.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in this case, Mr. Nice and Your Honours, you are accepting as an exhibit something that is provided as secondhand information by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, Colonel. Mr. Nice also said that the Albanians thought that they would be killed if they failed to leave. Now, tell me this, please: At that time, the material time that we're discussing and the time that you testified about and said that a large number of Albanians gathered together in the centre of Pec and that they left going off in different directions, now, was anybody killed? Was a single Albanian killed during that period, during those days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And we could -- were convinced of that looking at the list. We were able to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. One more question now. Actually, it was a question that Mr. Nice asked you with the fact that Albanians were allegedly deprived of their ID cards by the police. Did you or any of your colleagues, or any other policemen, for that matter, whom you happen to know, or any soldier whom you know, did they ever confiscate documents from Albanians?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PAPONJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't in our interest to confiscate documents. It was in our interest for people to possess documents so we could ascertain their identity to know who we were dealing with and who the people were. So there would have been no logic in us confiscating documents from people because we're the people issuing documents to citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. May I ask the interpreters just to return to that issue of relocating the people from or out of the zone. Could it be translated in any of the following ways: Relocating the people in the zone, relocating the people belonging to the zone, or relocating the people of the zone, or indeed relocating the zone people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that we have a look at the original again. All the examples are possible, however. The word used is "iz zone," meaning "from the zone." If it were "of the zone," it would be "stanovnistvo zone." But we suggest a proper expertise by the CLSS service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, with respect to this, I'd like to draw your attention to another few aspects of that particular sentence. The question here is of the population. It refers to the population - the word is "stanovnistvo" - and not to Albanians per se. That's the first point. The second point is this: In that same sentence it says that it is relocation in the interests of proper -- so that -- the proper functioning of life. Therefore, in the interests of the population. So that the explanation given by the witness is that this whole matter was undertaken in order to protect the population from the effects of armed activities, and that's the only explanation that can be deduced from that particular passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I thank the interpreters. We'll consult the CLSS. Mr. Paponjak, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I repeat my request to have these exhibits tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're going to consider that now. We're going to consider the exhibits now. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I repeat my argument, or state my argument that all of this material should be excluded. In addition to the more fundamental argument, this is an example of the impossibility of dealing with material without full and complete advance translation, for there is simply no realistic prospect of any of us returning to deal with these documents, exhibits in detail now that the witness has left, and no question of anyone seeking to have him come back, as far as I'm concerned. The fundamental objection comes from the mouth of the witness himself, and I'll give you, I think, two or three quotations of things he has said. I said to him, "Let me restate my question with the addition of one other clause. When you signed off all these documents in 2002, save and so far as the documents related to traffic police, you were in no position from your own knowledge to underwrite or guarantee the accuracy of those documents at all, were you?" To which he replied, "On the basis of my own personal knowledge, I could not."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have in this Chamber and in this Tribunal accepted evidence from witnesses who, in your words, cannot underwrite or guarantee the accuracy of documents which they present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite right. But we have to look at the detail of what comes from this witness to see which side of the acceptability line this material falls. He went on to say in answer to this particular question that for the head of the secretariat to be able to find something according to my question, it would appear he'd have to check every detail himself, to interview each criminal, to read through each of the documents. And the Chamber will recall that he made it quite plain that he'd done little if any of that at the time whatever the questions in re-examination, and that contrasts sharply with the position of those who have come to produce the large compilations who not only gave a detailed account of the method of preparation but also explained, I think, in each case that they had themselves done checking and verification of the material. He doesn't even suggest that he did that himself. Another of his answers was to this effect: "I did not personally compile any of these pieces of information. I said somewhere along the lines that the head of the Secretariat of the Interior can be equated with a manager." So he doesn't compile any documents. He doesn't interview any individuals. That's not his job. He doesn't study any documents. All he does is sign documents in his official capacity as an official. Now, that is completely different from and well short of any of the evidence that we've produced of this broadly, it may be very broadly, similar kind, and I would invite the Chamber to say that it simply falls the wrong side of the line, and very far the wrong side of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say he doesn't study any documents. What do you mean? You mean he hasn't read the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what he said. And he once more made it pretty plain he hadn't studied any of the documents. He claimed passing knowledge, for example, to one video at one stage, to the Salihaj papers, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, did you -- did he say that he didn't read the documents that he had signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He didn't say he hadn't read the documents he signed. He signed them. Although he certainly made it plain in relation to one of them that he hadn't drafted it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber has got to distinguish, of course, between the informations, that's the cover documents which are the sort of general conclusions and the supporting material, there's been a general pattern to all of that, and it was the document which referred to The Hague indictment that he was quite anxious, you may have concluded, to create a distance between. But he made it clear in his own answer: It's not his job. He doesn't study documents, all he does is sign documents in his official capacity as an official. And the Chamber will have remembered, observed today the quality of his knowledge of detail. For example, when the accused took him, without my conceding that it was even remotely appropriate to do so, but he did, to 7.2 point 69, a fascinating entry given that, as we now see, it comes on the 22nd of May, apparently, was clearly intended to support the accused's case on bombing on that date and yet deals with the burial of the bodies that on any reckoning occurred three days later. So that we have fundamentally flawed supporting material that the witness knew nothing about and didn't prepare. He was unable or unwilling to take the opportunity to name the people who compiled these documents, because I gave him that opportunity but he needed his rest and we left it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can it be said, Mr. Nice, that any of the witnesses that you presented to produce Human Rights Watch "Under Orders" studied the documents that they presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't have immediately to hand the full detail of their account but in each case their supervision of methodology was a great deal more detailed than this, and as I recall went into saying that they checked the underlying workings and material upon which they compiled their books, yes. This is completely different, and it is totally remote. He simply basically ultimately says, well, there was a group of people, they prepared a report and I signed off the cover documents. If you add that to the problems of translation, it's our respectful submission that this material simply shouldn't be admitted, and it will serve as an extremely helpful reminder to the accused that if he wishes to admit or have admitted material of this kind, not only must it be translated but its justification to be admitted must be more properly rooted. Your Honours, before I sit down may I make an entirely separate point dealing with the NATO bombing of Dubrava prison. I had a document that there was no point in putting to the witness because he wouldn't have been able to acknowledge it or deal with it, and therefore I didn't put it to him and waste time, but I do have a document that sets out from NATO the acknowledgement of the bombing on the 19th and 21st of May, with a list of the projectiles or missiles that were used on those occasions. It's in answer to a detailed question. It's a matter for Chamber in due course whether it would like to see it. I can, of course, go through the process of trying to produce it in the rebuttal case, but that case is already becoming concerningly large in contemplation and I'm also aware of the fact that by the time we get through to it a lot of time will pass. So if the Chamber's interested in seeing NATO's reply to the question of what bombs were dropped on those days, I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In considering this matter, it's worth looking at what is the essential investigative evidence produced by the Prosecution in relation to the crime scene of Dubrava. That evidence was produced by Dr. Eric Baccard who just put four files into the courtroom and answered about four questions, which I have here, as to gunshot wounds and explosive wounds, saying that 37 per cent of the people had gunshot wounds and over 40 per cent had explosive wounds. In his four files was contained a video taken by someone else, Jacky Rowland, who subsequently gave evidence, a detailed report by Spanish investigation team concerning the identities of corpses, which was none of his material or work, he just supervised the production of it into the courtroom, and then a detailed report by a Danish investigation team concerning the crime scene itself. Inside that report, there is material from someone described as a witness who gives descriptive events as to what had taken place and what was the -- what formed a basis for the investigation by the Danish team. That person isn't even named, he's just described as being a witness who describes a massacre taking part in one part and guides the Danish team around the building. As an example and a matter of reference, if you go to tab 9 of Exhibit 165, a document which is headed K0173927, under paragraph 3, has tactical information and sets out there what the witness states happened. So presumably the Trial Chamber will view this attaching what weight it feels appropriate. It won't be regarding it as being evidence taken under oath. And that's exactly the same set of circumstances we have with this witness Mr. Paponjak, who is coming into court in a very similar position to Mr. Baccard who produced a load of files from various other teams he had nothing to do with himself and just presented conclusions upon. It's actually the content of those files that is the important evidence in the case. We objected to that at the time, and it was ruled as being admissible evidence. Certain parts were taken out, such as the summarising statements by, for example, an investigator, Mr. Stewart, Nigel Stuart. That was taken out of the exhibits. But the content remained before the Trial Chamber. And the process undertaken by the accused in his Defence here is not dissimilar at all to that of the Prosecution. A large number of the exhibits are in fact prepared contemporaneously in 1999. One can see that from the materials. And the video that was produced is original material and exactly similar to that of Ms. Rowland who was the Prosecution witness whose film of the scene was sought to be brought into evidence and was successful by the Prosecution to be produced as an exhibit as being contemporaneous film of the time. So in my submission, the accused should be entitled to rely upon this material in exactly the same way as the Prosecutor was permitted to produce similar documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think any of the comments made by Mr. Nice can be acceptable, because after Mr. Nice, precisely because in the cross-examination he raised those questions, I clarified with the witness, that is to say -- or, rather, what he meant when he said he hadn't read. Does it mean that he hadn't read the details or that he stood or did not stand behind what it said then? He said that he stood behind all the documents in full that he signed, that he looked through them, that he had a series of cases before him to which the documents refer, which means that he stands by them in every respect. Mr. Nice would have it appear that Mr. Paponjak is somebody who said he signed these documents like a robot, anybody put in front of him by one of his staff. On the contrary, Mr. Paponjak is head of the Secretariat of the Interior for Pec, was at the head of the team, and he said that although he didn't write the documents himself that the whole team wrote them and worked on them, that he nonetheless controlled the team, signed the documents once he was convinced, to use your term, that beyond reasonable doubt the documents did in fact contain all the relevant facts and data and that they were grounded in the documents that the SUP had in its possession. So in every respect, he was the competent authority to testify about those documents. Mr. Nice says what is the basis for having them admitted into evidence? Well, the basis is that the witness was here, he was sitting in the courtroom; he was in Pec throughout, he was at the head of the team throughout working on these matters and compiling the documents, and because the witness is the person who signed all the documents that he testified about here. And Mr. Nice was not able to challenge any of the arguments put forward. So these are official documents belonging to the police force for the material time when the documents were compiled. So I don't think there is a single reason for not admitting those documents into evidence as exhibits. Mr. Nice also mentioned, for example, that there were attachments to the documents which the witness did not use on time. Now, these attachments mentioned by Mr. Nice are to be found in the tabs. So the witness might not have thought of referring to a tab or a document in a tab, but anyway all the attachments and attending material, whether they were used in response to the questions or not, have been disclosed and were placed within these binders before the witness started his testimony. So we cannot say for some documents that were before you, whether translated or not translated, that somebody wanted to skim over them or forget them altogether. The fact that the documents were presented in itself testifies to the fact that the intention was to tender them into evidence and to have the contents of those documents considered by you. Otherwise, as to the fact -- the comment made that it wasn't translated, I explained the difficulties we had in translating the material. So that argument can only be an argument in favour of something being admitted into evidence subsequently, once it has been translated, and to have them marked for identification in the meantime and not as an argument per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Generally the documents the Chamber found to be relevant and sufficiently reliable to be of probative value, and therefore they would be admitted. The question of weight to be attached to them is another matter. So there are three categories. Those documents that were translated will be admitted. Translated -- if they were used, those documents that were translated and which have been used in evidence are admitted. Those not translated and which were used we'll mark for identification pending translation. The third area, the documents that were not used will not be admitted. That comprises tabs 9, 11 to 19, 24 to 26, 28 to 32, 34, 35, 39, 41, 42, 44, 45, and 47 to 49. That's the ruling of the Chamber. We are adjourned until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in relation to your next witness, Mr. Stevanovic, I'd asked you to give us an indication as to the areas of the indictment to which the evidence will relate so that we can plan and prepare and follow the evidence more clearly, and I'd like you, first thing, to spend about five minutes telling us about the -- telling us about that.
